2611.10122.abstract: The H$_3^+$ molecular ion is the cornerstone of interstellar ion-molecule chemistry. Its vibrational transitions have long been observed, in absorption along many interstellar sight lines and in emission from the upper atmospheres of the giant planets, but its pure rotational spectrum, which consists only of "forbidden" transitions made possible by centrifugal distortion, had not been observed in the laboratory or in any astronomical source. With JWST/MIRI we have detected this spectrum toward the Herbig-Haro object HH 168 in Cepheus A West. Twenty-six lines are detected above 5 $\sigma$ in one or both of two fields, of which the (J,K) = (5,0) -> (4,3) line at 16.325 $\mu$m is the strongest. The H$_3^+$ lines share the velocity and spatial distribution of the hot shocked H$_2$, not of the ionized gas. A rotation diagram yields a rotational temperature of ~ 730 K, but the level populations are not thermal and are best explained by subthermal excitation in gas at > 2000 K. We compare the observations with models of shocks propagating into mildly irradiated molecular gas. Constrained by the H$_2$ rotational lines, a dissociative J-type shock predicts H$_3^+$ emission within a factor ~1.5 of that observed, while a nondissociative C-type shock, which fits the H$_2$ lines better, underpredicts it by a factor 5-6, although the excitation of H$_3^+$ by energetic collisions is poorly known. Archival MIRI data show the H$_3^+$ forbidden rotational spectrum in the HH 211 bow shock. The H$_3^+$ lines provide a new probe of the ionization in shocked molecular gas.

2611.10125.abstract: The methylidyne cation forms in warm or shocked interstellar gas through the endothermic reaction C$^+$ + H$_2$ -> CH$^+$ + H. Because C$^+$, which is common in irradiated and shocked gas, reacts with H$_2$ only when the reactants supply > 0.4 eV, CH$^+$ traces energy deposition in molecular gas. JWST/MIRI observations of HH 168 reveal the pure rotational lines R(17)-R(31) of CH$^+$ at 13.7-21.3 micron, from upper levels J = 18-32 (0.57-1.65 eV). Eleven lines exceed 5 sigma in both of the two fields that we observed and match the hot H$_2$ in radial velocity and spatial distribution. Because collisional excitation is negligible, each ion entering the v = 0 ladder emits one photon in every R(J) line below its entry level, so the line intensities provide the first measured rotational distribution of the ground-state products. The photon intensity falls almost linearly with increasing J, as expected for formation at a similar rate into every level up to J ~ 33; formation in J = 32 requires > 2 eV of reactant energy. The line positions, up to 150 km/s redward of ExoMol predictions, provide the first measurement of the CH$^+$ rotational intervals above J = 16. A Boltzmann distribution at $\phi T$ ~ 6200 K, where $\phi$ is the fraction of the available energy appearing in rotation, fits slightly better, implying reactant energies equivalent to several thousand kelvin. These lines probe the dynamics of a prototypical interstellar ion-molecule reaction.

2611.10127.abstract: We present a resolved star study of AM-1, a distant ($D \simeq 120$ kpc), faint ($M_V \sim -5.1$) Milky Way (MW) globular cluster, based on Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) imaging. To perform photometry of the Euclid VIS and NISP imaging, we develop a Euclid-specific module for the crowded field stellar photometry package DOLPHOT. We construct and present empirical point spread function (PSF) models for VIS and NISP, along with a photometric calibration, entirely from the public Q1 images. Our photometry reaches $5\sigma$ point source depths of $I_E, Y_E, J_E, H_E = 27.1, 25.3, 25.5, 25.3$, $\sim$1-1.5 mag deeper than the public Q1 catalog, as expected for dedicated resolved star PSF photometry. We resolve the cluster to $\sim$1 mag below its main sequence turnoff in all bands. The Euclid photometry agrees with color-magnitude diagram (CMD) modeling of archival HST/WFPC2 imaging and with the 2MASS-anchored VISTA Hemisphere Survey to $\lesssim0.02$ mag in $I_E$, $J_E$, and $H_E$, with a $\sim$0.07 mag offset in $Y_E$. We find that AM-1 hosts an old ($\sim$10.6 Gyr), intermediate-metallicity ([Fe/H] $\sim -1$) population, with a present-day stellar mass of $\sim 2\times10^4\,M_\odot$ and $M/L_V \simeq 2.2$, and has a half-light radius of $\sim$12-16 pc with a round, low-concentration profile. These affirm earlier studies placing AM-1 among the most extended, diffuse outer-halo clusters, which dynamical work identifies as accreted. We describe and publicly release DOLPHOT v2.1, the Euclid module, and its empirical PSFs, which together enable Euclid resolved star studies ranging from faint MW systems such as AM-1 to more luminous galaxies throughout the Local Volume. We anticipate further refinements, including spatially varying PSFs, with Euclid Data Release 1.

2611.10132.abstract: Classical Cepheids (CCs) are key distance indicators and tracers of young stellar populations in the Milky Way. Their period-luminosity-metallicity (PLZ) relation also makes them calibrators of the Hubble constant $H_0$. Despite their importance, chemical composition, especially non-LTE (NLTE) effects, remains a significant source of systematics in PLZ applications. In preparation for the large CCs sample expected from the 4MIDABLE-HR (4MOST Consortium Survey 4: Milky Way Disc and Bulge High-Resolution) survey, we present a method for deriving Cepheid atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances in NLTE. Using the Payne artificial neural network (ANN) trained on NLTE spectra, we derive atmospheric parameters and abundances for 17 elements: O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Ba, Eu in NLTE and C and Cr in LTE. We apply the new method to archival spectra of Cepheids and derive radial chemical gradients in the Milky Way. We derive robust NLTE stellar parameters and abundances for Cepheids spanning metallicities from $\sim -0.87$ to $\sim +0.35$ dex. For stars with multi-epoch spectra, we find that NLTE abundances are consistent across the pulsation cycle, whereas LTE values show larger dispersions and biases. The resulting abundance distributions and gradients align well with Galactic disk expectations from chemical evolution models. We confirm that the gradients flatten in the outer disk beyond $R_{\rm GC} \sim 15\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and provide the first NLTE gradients for Co, Ni, Y, and Eu. We show that our NLTE astrophysical analysis yields robust solutions for atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances across spectra at the resolving power of 4MOST-HR. This enables large, homogeneous studies with upcoming surveys such as 4MOST 4MIDABLE-HR and provides a solid basis for tightening constraints on Galactic chemical evolution models and Cepheid distance-scale work.

2611.10149.abstract: One of the main steps in data reduction for ground-based astronomy is sky subtraction. For extended objects, it is necessary to observe dedicated sky frames, usually with airmass values similar to the target's, using different pointing strategies. However, it is not well documented how different observing strategies can affect the science end product. In particular, with the use of the MUSE/VLT, this can yield distinct stellar population products, such as age, metallicity, and \alpha-enhancement. To address this, we considered two case studies seeking to investigate: (i) the sky stability in observations taken consecutively over a period of 2 hours with thin sky transparency and airmass values of 1.25-1.05, and (ii) the impact of different sky conditions on the same target. Among our main results, we find that for galaxies with 0.0014 < z < 0.0077, the sky line [NI] at \lambda 5200 coincides with the Mgb bandpass, which is essential for metallicity measurements, highlighting the need for proper sky subtraction. In addition, for regions with relative fluxes above 10 with respect to the sky in NGC1097, sky frames with variation up to ~18 % still retrieve consistent stellar population properties - in this case, this corresponds to flux values of >1500 x 10^-20 erg/s/cm^2 and Johnson-V ~19.0. In contrast, when comparing data from different nights for NGC1433, fainter regions suffer greatly from distinct sky conditions, especially in metallicity measurements, which range within +/- 0.2, strongly affecting the interpretation of stellar mass assembly and the origin of the gas (i.e., mergers might bring metal-poor gas, while an in-situ burst of star formation can yield metal-rich stars). This study is the first of its kind and highlights the importance of proper sky subtraction, providing insights regarding data limitations and observational strategies for future observations with MUSE.

2611.10419.abstract: Active galactic nuclei exhibit complex, nonlinear multiwavelength variability that standard cross-correlation techniques, sensitive only to linear covariance, may fail to capture fully. We apply time-lagged Mutual Information (MI) lag estimation, via the Kraskov-Stoegbauer-Grassberger $k$-nearest-neighbour estimator ($k = 5$) with a 150-iteration Random Subset Selection bootstrap, to the light curves of four Seyfert galaxies (Mrk 509, NGC 5548, NGC 4151, and NGC 4593) monitored across eight energy bands by Swift. In the UV/optical regime the MI estimator successfully reproduces the inter-band disc reprocessing lags established by the interpolated cross-correlation function, with performance degrading toward the optical where low variability amplitude produces poorly defined MI peaks. In the X-ray bands, where the physical X-ray/UV coupling is known to be weak, the estimator fails to recover consistent lags across the sample, with the notable exception of NGC 4593. Contextualising these outcomes within the multifractal characterisation of our previous work, we discuss how MI performance relates to the multifractal spectral width $\Delta\alpha$ of each band, and we propose $\Delta\alpha$ as a candidate diagnostic for anticipating where MI-based reverberation mapping is likely to succeed or fail in multiband datasets of active galactic nuclei.

2611.10456.abstract: The transition from atomic hydrogen (HI) to molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the first step in the evolution from diffuse interstellar gas to dense star-forming cores. HI narrow self-absorption (HINSA), produced by cold atomic gas mixed with molecular material, provides a direct tracer of the HI-to-H$_2$ transition in molecular clouds. Existing HINSA analyses typically model HINSA as a single Gaussian component with a uniform spin temperature. This approach cannot recover the radial HI distribution and yields large errors for young cores whose profiles deviate from a Gaussian shape. Here we present hinspheres, an open-source framework that models the core as onion-like spherically symmetric concentric shells, solves radiative transfer along the line of sight and jointly fits the HI abundance, temperature, and kinematic parameters. The framework recovers all parameters with a mean relative error of 4.6-6.8% on our synthetic data with different ages. A combined resolution-noise grid shows that the median recovery error remains below 16% for cores within 1 kpc observed at FAST resolution with noise levels below 0.2 K. Applying it to the dark cores L1574 and L1544, we reveal radial HI abundance profiles that span about three orders of magnitude, which were missed by the single-Gaussian method. The derived chemical ages are $6.5\times10^6$ and $8.7\times10^6$ yr, respectively. Compared with the commonly used single-Gaussian method, hinspheres characterizes the radial profile of HINSA structures more accurately, making it well suited to identifying and analyzing young cores undergoing the HI-to-H$_2$ transition.

2611.10548.abstract: The Milky Way exhibits a hierarchical structure shaped by mergers, accretion, and internal dynamics. Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) enables a global view of this structure, but requires scalable, model-agnostic methods to extract multi-scale clustering patterns. We aim to characterise the hierarchical clustering structure of the Milky Way in a model-agnostic way and to assess how the resulting structures relate to existing catalogues. We apply the hierarchical density-based clustering algorithm AstroLink to a locally magnitude-complete subsample of over one billion Gaia DR3 stars with five-dimensional astrometric information. The data are corrected for selection effects and transformed using a distance contraction and feature scaling. We compare the resulting cluster hierarchy to catalogues of open clusters, globular clusters, dwarf galaxies, and stellar streams using custom availability-aware metrics and a bi-directional best-match framework. At a significance threshold of $S = 3.8\sigma$, AstroLink identifies 7410 statistically significant clusters spanning a wide range of morphologies. Compact systems are often recovered as reciprocal matches with many also exhibiting internal substructure, while extended structures are typically fragmented or partially recovered. A substantial fraction of clusters have no counterpart in the comparison catalogues, these may be new structures but additional physical checks are needed to verify this. A model-agnostic, hierarchical clustering approach can recover the multi-scale structure of the Milky Way at Gaia DR3 scale and provides a unified framework for comparing heterogeneous catalogues and identifying candidate structures.

2611.10910.abstract: The Tully--Fisher relation (TFR) and the specific angular momentum--mass relation (SAMR) link the baryonic content of a disc to its kinematics and dynamics. Hence, these scaling relations should bear the imprints of any process removing baryons or altering their kinematics, such as those acting in clusters of galaxies. We test this using the MUSE survey "GAs Stripping Phenomena in galaxies" (GASP), which targets field, group, and cluster members at $z \approx 0.05$ and various stages of ram pressure stripping. For the 81 discs with favourable inclinations, we measure the distribution and kinematics of stars and ionised gas, and their specific angular momenta. Within their scatter, the stellar and baryonic relations show no significant dependence on the large scale environment: the TFRs have slopes $\alpha \approx 3.6$ and $\approx 3.5$ for any kinematic tracer, and the SAMRs have $\alpha \approx 0.65$--$0.75$, as predicted by tidal torque theory. The same holds for the ten S0-S0/as in our sample, consistent with the "faded spiral" formation scenario. Only the gas SAMR shows an environmental signature, with ram pressure stripped galaxies lying $\approx 0.16$~dex below unperturbed ones. This offset is mostly due to their enhanced star formation rate, and thus higher gas mass when inferred through the Schmidt-Kennicutt law, rather than to kinematic perturbations or disc truncation. Our results suggest that, within the area probed by MUSE ($\lesssim6$ disc scale lengths), these discs have preserved the angular momentum acquired at formation not only from cluster processes and pre-processing in filaments, but also from mergers and ejective feedback acting in any environment.

2611.10979.abstract: Past observations and simulations have shown that the bar in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) may be tilted with respect to the disk plane, and that the outer LMC disk could be warped. These studies propose that the tilted bar and the warp in the LMC are induced by the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) pericentric passages. We analyze and quantify the effect of the SMC passage on the vertical position and kinematic asymmetries of both the bar and disk, as a function of different impact parameters or initial conditions. We used seven representative simulations from the KRATOS suite of $N$-body simulations of the LMC, SMC and Milky Way (MW) system for this analysis. To classify bar particles and analyze the bar and disk separately, we adopted a classification method based on persistent homology. To quantify the vertical asymmetries in the bar and disk of the LMC-like galaxy, we applied Fourier decomposition. We constructed Gaia DR3 mock catalogs to study whether the observed vertical asymmetries in Gaia DR3 are caused by astrometric uncertainties. We detect strong $m = 1$ vertical asymmetries in the bar and disk of the LMC-like galaxy for all interacting simulations after the pericentric passage of the SMC-like galaxy, indicative of a warped bar and disk. We also detect $m=2$ vertical asymmetries in the bar of the LMC-like galaxy for some simulations, indicative of a buckling bar. We conclude that the SMC passages induce vertical asymmetries in both the bar and the disk of the LMC, compatible to those measured in Gaia DR3. Tidal interactions naturally give rise to a warped and buckling LMC bar, and a warped LMC disk. Comparison between our results and Gaia DR3 suggest that models with a higher mass ratio between the SMC and the LMC may be favorable for reproducing the observed tilt of the LMC bar, and that the most recent SMC pericentric passage occurred at most 210 to 300 Myr ago.

2611.11075.abstract: We investigate possible causal influences in five historical seasons (1989-1993) of NGC 5548 using a version of the Synergistic-Unique-Redundant Decomposition (SURD) method adapted for this analysis, an information-theoretic causal discovery method for time series. Two four-variable sets contain the blue wing (B), core (C) and red wing (R) of H-beta together with either total H-beta (H) or the 5100 Angstrom continuum (F). We examine 7200 decompositions with common and unequal lags, two or three seasonal flux states, and base delays of 1-30 d. We rank the individual named components within each information family, reporting their amplitudes and simultaneous leakage. In 1989, unique continuum information about the core reaches 0.799 and 0.387 of target entropy for two and three states, with leakage 0.047 and 0.276. In 1992, the red-wing history supplies unique information about the future blue wing in both variable sets and both state counts, with peak target-entropy fractions 0.106-0.166. Distinct joint influences also emerge: for the 1991 core, the two-state S(F,B) and S(F,R) components contribute 0.187 and 0.125 at 20 d with leakage 0.087, although the unique continuum term vanishes. Strong core-wing redundancy identifies candidate inputs for simpler predictive models. Large late-lag leakage, reaching approximately 0.97 in the total set, identifies targets for additional driver measurements and richer temporal histories. The resulting seasonal map of individual, shared and joint influences complements the response delays and velocity structure measured by reverberation mapping, and provides specific causal hypotheses for the evolving broad-line region.

2611.11078.abstract: We have observed the fullerene-rich planetary nebula Tc 1 with the MIRI/MRS on JWST. The mid-infrared spectra of this spatially resolved source reveal that the dust emission is not co-spatial with the fullerene emission. Three broad features can be distinguished: a 6$\unicode{x2013}$9 $\mu$m plateau, a 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $\mu$m plateau and the 30 $\mu$m feature. The 6$\unicode{x2013}$9 $\mu$m plateau does not change shape spectrally across the entire field of view, indicating it is produced by stochastically heated material. Spectral variations of the 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $\mu$m plateau reveal at least three distinct components, peaking at 9.5 $\mu$m, 11 $\mu$m and 12 $\mu$m respectively. SiC produces most likely at least the 11 $\mu$m component and we find evidence that the 12 $\mu$m component might be produced by SiC grains too. The variation in relative strength of these components across the field of view hints at dust processing taking place in Tc 1. The 9.5 $\mu$m component of the 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $\mu$m plateau has a strong correlation with the SiC component(s) and is thus likely produced by similar material.

2611.11107.abstract: We present deep 1.26 GHz radio continuum observations of the two $z=2.24$ protoclusters BOSS1244 and BOSS1542 with the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) to investigate their members' radio emission and its possible environmental dependence. Among 187 and 105 H$\alpha$ emitter (HAE) members in BOSS1244 and BOSS1542, we identify ten and two robust radio counterparts, respectively, together with five potential counterparts from forced photometry. Two HAEs and the massive quiescent galaxy QG1 in BOSS1244 show strong radio excesses relative to their H$\alpha$-based star formation rates (SFRs) and are identified as strong radio-excess AGN candidates. Median stacking of the remaining 173 and 102 radio-undetected HAE members yields positive signals at $2.8\sigma$ and $3.2\sigma$ in BOSS1244 and BOSS1542, respectively. The stacked radio luminosities are consistent with those expected from the median H$\alpha$-based SFRs, indicating that star formation can account for the average faint radio emission. After excluding the robust radio counterparts, we divided the HAE members by the projected distance from QG1 in BOSS1244 and from the filament spine in BOSS1542. The largest stacked radio luminosities are found toward the denser regions in both systems, but the differences are not statistically significant, and stellar mass shows no significant dependence on environmental distance. These results identify strong radio-excess AGN candidates among the individually detected members, while the faint HAE population is on average consistent with radio emission from star formation. The similar environmental ordering is suggestive but remains tentative. Deeper radio observations at multiple frequencies and higher angular resolution are required to determine whether this apparent trend reflects weak AGN activity or variations in radio emission associated with star formation.

2611.11440.abstract: Hubble Frontier Field cluster Abell 370 ($z=0.375$) has been the target of a suite of legacy multi-wavelength observational campaigns and is a prime candidate to host a diffuse radio halo, given its high mass ($\sim10^{15}\,\rm{M_\odot}$) and non-relaxed dynamical state. Previous detections of its radio halo were of low significance and imaging fidelity, leading to an uncertain characterisation of its nature. We use deep MeerKAT Ultra-High Frequency observations ($580-1015\,\rm{MHz}$) to robustly map the halo's spatial extent and spectral properties. We find a radio emission size of $\sim 1.1\,\rm{Mpc}$, significantly larger than previously reported. We measure a MeerKAT UHF in-band integrated spectral index of $\alpha=-1.54\pm0.05$. This result is consistent with an ultra-steep spectrum radio halo ($\alpha\lesssim-1.5$). We find a strong, sub-linear correlation ($k=0.60\pm0.08$) between the radio and X-ray surface brightness. The radio halo's position on the $P_{1.4\,\rm{GHz}}-M_{500}$ scaling relation is underluminous, consistent with the known USSRH population. The combined evidence strongly supports that the diffuse central radio emission in Abell 370 is an Ultra-Steep Spectrum Radio Halo (USSRH), refining its previous classification and providing further support for the turbulent re-acceleration model.

2611.12047.abstract: We use a suite of hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations of Milky Way analogues to investigate how previously identified trends in dust properties of galaxies can be utilised to infer the underlying dark matter model. We use a sample of 24 comparison simulations comparing a cold dark matter (CDM) and 3.5 keV warm dark matter (WDM) particle, primarily using a dust-to-metals (DTM) ratio to post-process the dust in the simulation, with alternative methods explored. We find a preference for higher dust masses in CDM over WDM, with a median increase of 6.6 per cent in the CDM sample at redshift $z=0$, and with a peak median difference of 25 per cent at $z\approx0.25$. Both CDM and WDM samples are highly concentrated, with approximately 90 per cent of the dust located in the inner region of the halo, though slightly higher in CDM. Contrary to previous work, we find that the Gini coefficient does not consistently show a difference in comparisons of dark matter models, with differences primarily driven by high sensitivity to the unique structure of individual haloes. Finally, we conduct an analysis of some common dust scaling relations, finding that the differences between the two samples in the dust-to-stellar mass and dust-to-SFR functions do not constitute a statistically significant difference at $z=0$ with any dust production mechanism. However, at redshifts where the difference in dust mass is greatest, the alternative dust production methods show larger separations between CDM and WDM samples in total mass and scaling relations.

2611.12147.abstract: With their star formation efficiencies (SFE) and star formation rates (SFR) falling between normal star-forming galaxies and starbursts (SBs), ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) at intermediate redshifts ($0.2<z<1$) have been postulated to be good probes of galaxies transitioning between these two regimes. Here, we present new Atacama Large Millimetre Array (ALMA) observations of a representative sample of 22 ULIRGs at redshifts $0.46<z<0.81$ evenly distributed across dust temperature ranges of $25<T_{\rm dust}<50~K$ and spanning infrared luminosities of $10^{12.0}<L_\text{IR}<10^{12.7}~L_\odot$. We detected CO(2-1) emission in 14 of these galaxies (64%). The SFE of these 14 targets are all similar, corresponding to depletion timescales on the order of hundreds of Myr. By employing two different versions of the main sequence relation of galaxies -- one based on the specific SFR (sSFR) and one based on directly observable parameters (CO and IR luminosities) -- we statistically confirm that the present sample of intermediate redshift ULIRGs indeed lies in the transitional region between MS and SB galaxies. In addition, we establish that the SFE of our sample of ULIRGs is a strong indicator of the position of a galaxy relative to the MS and the SB branches. Based on the observed morphologies and star-forming properties, we suggest that minor mergers provide a viable mechanism for temporarily enhancing the SFR and SFE of intermediate-redshift ULIRGs, although other evolutionary phases and pathways cannot be excluded.

2611.12284.abstract: We present H$\alpha$ luminosity function (LF) measurements at redshifts $z\sim1.3$ and $z\sim2.0$. We adopt JWST grism data in five lensing cluster fields and their parallel fields from the CANUCS program: ABELL-370, MACS-J0416, MACS-J0417, MACS-J1149, MACS-J1423. Based on emission lines spectroscopically identified in the F115W, F150W and F200W filters, our final sample consists of 762 H$\alpha$ emitters, including 433 at $1.1<z<1.5$ and 329 at $1.8<z<2.2$. Through detailed effective volume and completeness analysis for each source, we construct the H$\alpha$ LF in two redshift bins. Thanks to the sensitivity of NIRISS WFSS and gravitational lensing magnification, our sample reaches intrinsic H$\alpha$ luminosities down to $L_{\rm H\alpha}\sim10^{40.6}~\rm erg~s^{-1}$ at $z\sim1.3$ and $L_{\rm H\alpha}\sim10^{41}~\rm erg~s^{-1}$ at $z\sim2.0$ with completeness larger than 80\%. The larger survey volume and coverage of multiple independent sightlines help mitigate cosmic variance. After accounting for cosmic variance, we constrain the faint-end slopes to be $\alpha_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}=-1.51^{+0.06}_{-0.04}$ at $z\sim1.3$ and $-1.42^{+0.09}_{-0.06}$ at $z\sim2.0$, indicating a mild evolution between the two redshift bins. We find a negligible contribution from bright active galactic nuclei in our sample. We estimate integrated cosmic star formation rate densities of $0.103^{+0.008}_{-0.007}~M_{\odot}~\rm yr^{-1}~Mpc^{-3}$ at $z\sim1.3$ and $0.149^{+0.016}_{-0.013}~M_{\odot}~\rm yr^{-1}~Mpc^{-3}$ at $z\sim2.0$. The emission-line samples presented here will enable further detailed studies of galaxy properties including metallicities. The methodology presented here can be readily applicable to other JWST slitless spectroscopic datasets and future wide-field slitless surveys, including those from Euclid, Roman, and the Chinese Space Station Telescope.

2611.12448.abstract: We present a spectroscopic study of the lensed quasar Q2237+0305, the Einstein Cross, assessing the best wavelength coverage to date with the X-shooter instrument (from $3000$ to $20000$ $\mathring{A}$), and thus improving the available spectroscopic data for this system. Using as a reference the characteristic emission lines for each quasar macro-image, we estimate the chromatic microlensing effect between pairs of images and calculate the extinction curve, confirming no significant differences between spectra $C$ and $A$ caused by extinction in the lens galaxy. In addition, we model the accretion disk characterized by a temperature profile with logarithmic slope $1/p$ and size $r_{s}$, assuming a thin-disk model with a power-law function of the form $r_{s}$ $\propto$ $\lambda^{p}$. To do this, we calculated a set of three chromatic microlensing measurements compiling previous estimates from the literature to test the wavelength dependence. This temperature profile was also compared to the canonical thin-disk model with $p=4/3$. Finally, we estimated the likelihood between the disk model and the observed data collected from multiple epochs through mock microlensing magnification maps and determined the probability density functions of each parameter from a Bayesian analysis. As a result, our estimated values for the accretion disk size and its exponential index are $r_{s}=4.9^{+2.3}_{-2.6}$ $\sqrt{M/0.3M_{\odot}}$ (lt-day) and $p=0.77^{+0.47}_{-0.28}$, respectively, reinforcing a departure from the standard accretion disk model ($ T \propto r_s^{-3/4}$).

2611.12470.abstract: The spatial stellar distribution in massive central galaxies preserves a stratified fossil record of their host halos' assembly history. Using a halo-mass-complete sample from the IllustrisTNG-300 hydrodynamical simulation at $z=0.4$, we quantify this connection with two diagnostics. The fossil correlation $\tilde{\rho}(z)$ measures how strongly a present-day galaxy property retains information about the progenitor halo mass at each redshift. The rank retention fraction $f_{\rm ret}(z)$ measures how many halos selected by that property today were among the most massive halos at each epoch. The central stellar mass at different galactocentric radii exhibits non-monotonic fossil correlations with past halo mass, peaking at intermediate redshifts that systematically shift from $z\sim1$ in the inner regions to $z\sim0.7$ in the outer stellar halos. These peak redshifts are robust from group to cluster scales. Partial correlations with halo accretion rate show that each peak marks the end of the epoch when that component's buildup was sensitive to halo accretion. The rank retention fraction shows that the annular stellar masses of the central galaxy beyond 10 kpc are less biased tracers of the most massive halos at intermediate redshifts than richness. This stratified fossil record originates mainly from the ex-situ phase of galaxy assembly. The outer stellar halo also traces the satellite population at intermediate redshift better than present-day richness. These results establish that the stellar profile of massive central galaxies encodes a radially stratified fossil record of halo assembly history.

2611.12734.abstract: The stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR), a key prediction of galaxy formation models, peaks at $M_* \sim 3 \times 10^{10}\,M_\odot$. This scale is often attributed to circumgalactic baryonic feedback processes, however, direct observational evidence linking the two remains scarce. Using Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) galaxy--quasar pairs, we map the cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) using Mg II $\lambda\lambda2796, 2803$ absorption with stacking technique across nearly three decades in stellar mass. The radial Mg II absorption equivalent-width profile, $W_{\rm MgII} \propto D^k$, becomes progressively shallower with increasing stellar mass, following $k = 0.70\log(M_*/M_\odot)-9.12$. Crucially, we find that the $W_{\rm MgII}$ in the CGM scales tightly with the SHMR. The $W_{\rm MgII}$ peaks at the same characteristic mass as the SHMR, coinciding with a transition of the cool CGM from super-virial to sub-virial kinematics. Low-mass halos show excess non-gravitational motions consistent with recycled accretion and feedback-driven circulation, whereas massive halos show halo-centric heating that may maintain star formation quenching. This study bridges the gap between cool CGM and SHMR, showing that peak star formation efficiency coincides with the most abundant cool CGM reservoirs.

2611.12846.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission is a powerful tool for the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) in both Galactic and extragalactic contexts. It can reveal ionization state, radiation field, metallicity, composition, and ISM structure as sculpted by processes like turbulence and stellar feedback. Here we use NASA's SPHEREx to produce clean, high-resolution PAH maps at spectral resolution R $\sim$ 35 (compared to WISE at R $\sim$ 2). Prior treatments of the SPHEREx linear variable filter data seek to convert them to more conventional band-averaged maps that can leave striping artifacts associated with spatially variable wavelength sampling, especially at emission lines. In contrast, we deliver a scalable forward-modeling method capable of generating high-quality all-sky SPHEREx emission-line maps at 8.5 arcsec FWHM angular resolution (on 6.4 arcsec pixels), while naturally producing maps without visible striping. We reformat the data into a pixel-level database, mask stellar contamination, and infill missing pixels with a conditional, data-driven, anisotropic Gaussian process. We apply our method to produce 3.3 $\mu$m and 3.4 $\mu$m PAH and Paschen-$\alpha$ emission maps of a set of fields spanning a range of Galactic and extragalactic conditions including the Rosette nebula, the Corona Australis molecular cloud, M33, and M31. We demonstrate the quality and synergies of our SPHEREx 3.3 $\mu$m PAH maps by comparisons with other available gas and dust tracer maps and achieve sensitivities up to $\sigma(I_{3.3}) = 2.7 \times 10^{-8}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$. We estimate that a two-year extension of the SPHEREx survey, with modest modifications to the scanning strategy, would match or exceed the PAH sensitivity of WISE over the whole sky.

2611.12860.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) probe foreground ionized baryons via their dispersion measures (DM). Using 1748 sub-arcminute-localized sources from the Second CHIME/FRB Baseband Catalog, we conduct a statistical stacking study of the circumgalactic media (CGM) of nearby galaxies by analyzing the DMs of FRBs whose sightlines intersect foreground halos. For galaxy halos within 50 Mpc, we measure a mean DM excess of $119\pm44$ pc~cm$^{-3}$ $(p = 0.0053; \sim 2.6\sigma)$ within one virial radius. Expanding to 150 Mpc (628 intersections), we find a tentative decline in the mean DM as a function of impact parameter $(p = 0.0046; \sim 2.6\sigma)$, which is predominantly driven by typical Milky Way (MW)-like galaxies $(10 \leq \log(M_*/M_\odot)\leq 11)$. We use this DM profile to constrain parameters of the CGM electron density distribution, $n_e^\mathrm{CGM}(r) \propto r^{-3\beta}$, finding an extrapolated central electron density in the range of $(1.7-21.1) \times 10^{-3}\mathrm{\,cm}^{-3}$, with a radial power-law index of $\beta = 0.68^{+0.15}_{-0.16}$, consistent with constraints from X-ray stacking studies of MW-like galaxies. At very low impact parameters, we detect a significant DM deficit likely due to cross-matching FRBs that originate from galaxies within our galaxy sample. By deriving the DM-galaxy cross-correlation function, we show that this deficit matches theoretical predictions if 20 FRBs originate from galaxies within 150 Mpc, indicating that CHIME/FRB detects a higher fraction of low-$z$ FRBs than previously thought. We forecast that $10^4$ FRBs with similar localization errors will provide a 5-$\sigma$ detection of the CGM, and that FRBs at intermediate redshifts ($0.4\lesssim z_\mathrm{FRB}\lesssim 0.75$) are ideal for studying intervening CGMs.

2611.10102.abstract: Although significant progress has been made over recent decades, a comprehensive and predictive framework for galaxy formation remains elusive. Starting from cosmological initial conditions, current models cannot a priori accurately predict key galaxy properties such as their structure, size, star formation histories, chemical abundance patterns, or supermassive black hole mass. This challenge stems from the vast range of spatial scales involved, as numerical simulations must simultaneously account for sub-AU processes nearby stars and black holes in addition to Mpc-scale cosmological gas inflows/outflows and environmental effects. Consequently, simulations must rely on subgrid models and approximations. As a result, theoretical progress in galaxy formation remains fundamentally driven by observational data and the iterative testing of model predictions against empirical results. Here we highlight five key open problems in theoretical galaxy formation that require dedicated observations of the high-redshift Universe, beyond what can currently be achieved through GO programs.

2611.10140.abstract: Hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae (H-rich SLSNe) are rare, exceptionally luminous transients. Most exhibit narrow Balmer emission and can be further classified as SLSNe-IIn, indicating interaction with dense circumstellar material (CSM). We present and analyse 304 optical spectra of 106 H-rich SLSNe observed by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). We examine their spectral evolution and Balmer-line properties, and model the H$\alpha$ profiles using Monte Carlo electron-scattering calculations. Of the 106 objects, 105 exhibit narrow Balmer emission consistent with SLSN-IIn classifications, including six with additional Ia-CSM-like characteristics and three with possible flash-ionisation features; the remaining one object exhibits only broad Balmer emission and is classified as a SLSN-II. Post-peak Balmer profiles range from approximately symmetric, exponential profiles to asymmetric profiles with prominent blue excesses or shoulders. Objects with Balmer line blue excess favour higher fitted photon-emitting shell velocities and tend to be fainter than those with persistently symmetric profiles. The H$\alpha$ pseudo-equivalent width (pEW) and FWHM of SLSNe-IIn overlap with those of lower-luminosity SNe IIn, while the pEW evolution is more diverse than in the broad-lined SLSN-II comparison sample. Our SLSNe-IIn sample's median Balmer decrement increases from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterwards, remaining consistently below that of the comparison Ia-CSM sample. We identify no Balmer-line morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn in the available comparison with lower-luminosity SNe IIn, although some SLSNe-IIn exhibit prolonged high-ionisation emission. Our results also support interaction with dense CSM formed through enhanced pre-explosion mass loss. We also highlight a possible hidden Ia-CSM population among luminous H-rich interacting SNe.

2611.10220.abstract: Type II supernovae (SNe) at 1-3yr after explosion can document not only the preSN mass loss history of massive stars but also the chemistry of the inner ejecta rich in metals and eventually molecules and dust. With the aim of modeling SN1987A, we present a grid of radiative-transfer models of Type II SNe at Zsun/3, covering an initial mass range between 11 and 21Msun, a fixed ejecta kinetic energy of 1.2e51erg, and ~0.08Msun of 56Ni. The influence of metallicity at such late times is found to be relatively weak. In this model set, the [OI]6330A flux at 1-2yr varies non-monotonically with Minit. It first rises with Minit due to the growing O abundance but drops for M>17-19Msun due to the higher ejecta density, with little change to the rest of the optical spectrum. Assuming CO molecules account for 90% of the cooling in the C/O shell leads to a 10-20% reduction in the [OI] flux, equivalent to an O(1Msun) reduction in Minit at M<19Msun. The fractional [OI] flux rises from 200 to ~600d but decreases beyond. We obtain a good agreement to SN1987A for all Minit apart from [OI], which appears in the optical as the only discriminant between models. The 13Msun model yields the best match, from UV to IR, but a higher Minit may result with allowance for strong CO and SiO cooling. Past 500d, a growing amount of dust below ~2000km/s is essential to account for the ~1.5mag optical excess fading relative to predictions from decay power. Adopting 0.1mic silicate grains, we find a dust mass of 1e-4Msun at 600d rising to a few 1e-3Msun at 700-800d. We also found that the 200-800d International Ultraviolet Explorer spectra of SN1987A are all contaminated by a background hot star, which also causes the relative UV brightening past 500d. Such contamination may complicate the interpretation of more distant SNe II at >~2yr once or if they fade to O(1e5Lsun) [abridged].

2611.10374.abstract: We present the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array Band 7 observations of the hyperfine structure of C$^{17}$O (3-2) and the H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$ (4-3) molecular line emissions of the Class 0 protostellar system HH 212 at $\sim$ 44 au spatial resolution. Radiative transfer models interpreted in the framework of non-ideal MHD of the envelope allow us to estimate an envelope mass of $M_{env}\sim0.12\,M_\odot$ and a mass infall rate of $\dot{M}_{env}\sim4.4-5.7\times10^{-6}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, consistent with values reported in the literature. The models also reveal a systematic radial velocity drift between the neutral tracer (C$^{17}$O (3-2)) and the ionized species (H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$ (4-3)) of $0.1-0.3$ km s$^{-1}$, exceeding the spectral resolution of 0.105 km s$^{-1}$ and consistent with possible ambipolar diffusion in the envelope. The ambipolar diffusion fraction, $f_{AD}\sim 0.1-1$, and the Hall parameter, $\beta_{i,H_2}\gg1$, indicate partial ion-neutral decoupling, with non-ideal effects becoming more significant toward the inner regions. In the envelope, our analysis shows that rotational energy decreases from $\sim 50\,\%$ of the gravitational energy at $R_{cen}$ to $\sim 25\,\%$ at $2R_{cen}$ and $\sim4\,\%$ at 1100 au. In contrast, for $B_0=1$ mG, magnetic energy increases from $\sim 0.4\,\%$ of the gravitational energy at $R_{cen}$ to $\sim2.6\,\%$ at $2R_{cen}$ and $\sim20\,\%$ at 1100 au. The drift velocity expected from radial force balance is consistent with the modeled drift velocity within $\sim300-400$ au of the central source but is lower at larger radii. These results are consistent with a scenario in which ambipolar diffusion leads to partial ion-neutral decoupling, allowing neutrals to move faster than ions within the envelope.

2611.10934.abstract: A stellar-mass black hole (BH) that collides with a massive star can be captured by drag and settle at its center as a black hole star. Hydrodynamic simulations that neglect nuclear reactions have found that the star survives and becomes a black hole star (BH*) for BH-to-star mass ratios $q\lesssim0.2$. We perform hydrodynamic simulations of head-on collisions with the \athenak\ code, including CNO burning coupled to the gas, for $q=0.1$ and $0.2$ BHs, stellar masses of $100$ and $500\,M_{\odot}$, solar, metal-deficient, and Helium-rich compositions. In all models (with $q\le0.2$), the energy dissipated by drag is comparable to or less than the binding energy that the captured BH adds to the gas so that it alone does not disrupt the star. But, under compression around the captured BH, gas is heated to $\gtrsim2\times10^8$\,K and undergoes thermonuclear burning at the $\beta$-limited hot-CNO rate. Within about one dynamical time after the BH settles at the center, the nuclear energy released during the encounter becomes a significant fraction of the star's binding energy $\tfrac32\bar{\beta}\int P\,dV$. The star loses most of its mass once the cumulative release reaches this binding energy. Below this threshold, the release rate declines. Merger between a solar-composition star and a BH with a mass ratio $q=0.2$ leads to the disruption of the star after releasing most of its total mass. But a metal-poor star, with nearly the same binding energy and total yield, survives with minor release after merger with an identical BH. After coalescence with a less massive ($q=0.1$) BH, stars with both solar and metal-poor composition survive as black hole stars, burning at a rate $\gtrsim 10^{44}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$, far from thermal equilibrium. Very massive and helium-rich stars, which are weakly bound, are the most easily disrupted.

2611.11617.abstract: The Galactic Center is home to the largest known concentration of X-ray sources ever detected in our Galaxy, including a sizable population of accreting compact objects. Utilizing data from the XMM-Newton Galactic Plane Heritage Survey of the central $20^{\circ}\times2^{\circ}$ of the Milky Way, we investigate the varying source populations in the inner regions of the Galaxy. We identify for the first time a concentration of extremely hard X-ray sources within $|l|<1.3^{\circ}$ and $|b|<0.3^{\circ}$, a region that overlaps the nuclear stellar disk (NSD). We determine that this hardness is intrinsic to the sources and not a manifestation of high line-of-sight column density ($N_{\rm H}$). Unlike the "soft" X-ray sources, this population does not trace the stellar mass distribution, indicating an overabundance compared to the underlying stellar population. We simulate spectra for a variety of source types to model their X-ray hardness and compare their distributions to those we observed in our survey data. We find that a significant subset of the Galactic Center X-ray population may comprise intermediate polars (IPs) with massive white dwarfs, possibly formed through dynamical processes. Our study provides novel observational insights into the distribution of stellar remnants and other X-ray sources in the vicinity of our supermassive black hole, Sgr A*.

2611.12015.abstract: Additive separation of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation depends on the Hamiltonian and on the canonical variables, and this paper introduces a five-input Poisson-bracket operator whose values on canonical pairs reproduce the Levi-Civita separability expressions. On a symplectic product structure its off-diagonal values are intrinsic, since they equal a symplectic pairing of the sector Hamiltonian fields and measure the Frobenius obstruction of a Lagrangian distribution, and their vanishing yields a local separation theorem. Because the operator is cubic in the Hamiltonian, its perturbation expansion is exact and defines a linearised separability operator and a defect functional. For Hamiltonians with a cyclic angle, the linearised operator divided by the squared rotor frequency is an angle derivative of the Melnikov integrand, so that the defect integrated along a homoclinic orbit decides the first-order splitting of the separatrix. Closed-form defects are obtained for the polar-nodal normal forms of satellite theory and, through a covariance of the operator on level sets, for Kerr geodesics. Used for coordinate selection, the defect singles out the separating focal distance of the Euler two-centre problem as its unique nondegenerate minimum, and for axisymmetric potentials it shows that the prescriptions of Sanders and Vasiliev are two weightings of the same Stäckel residual. The residual selector and Binney's shell-orbit fit improve both actions over the median prescription for 48 and 50 of 50 orbits in a flattened logarithmic potential, whereas the operator selector lowers the 90th-percentile action spread of 50 orbits in a Miyamoto-Nagai potential from 2.90% to 0.91%.

2611.12220.abstract: We present the first measurement of the variation of the high-energy neutrino flux along the Galactic plane using 10 years of neutrino-induced particle-shower data from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. In this Letter, we fit both the neutrino flux normalization and the spectral index, in multiple regions along the plane, independent of model expectations. The neutrino flux per solid angle in the inner Galactic region ($\vert l\vert< 30^{\circ}, \vert b\vert < 8^{\circ}$) is approximately five times higher than in the outer Galactic plane ($\vert l\vert>60^{\circ}, \vert b\vert < 8^{\circ}$) at $E_u=5\mathrm{TeV}$. The spectral indices in the inner and outer region are $\gamma=2.76^{+0.18}_{-0.15}$ and $\gamma = 3.13^{+0.57}_{-0.37}$, respectively. Additionally, we compare the same region of Galactic emission measured in $\mathrm{TeV}$ gamma rays by LHAASO ($15^{\circ}<l<125^{\circ}$) to neutrinos, and conclude that the measurements are compatible within uncertainties, under the assumption of hadronic gamma-ray production.

2611.12496.abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will provide novel capability to discover and study intermediate-mass (~$10^2-10^5 M_\odot$) black holes at the centres of dwarf galaxies and in dense stellar environments. We systematically map out the LISA-detectable parameter space of binaries consisting of a low-mass compact object spiralling into an intermediate-mass black hole (mass ratio ~$10^{-5} - 10^{-2}$) on equatorial orbits with generic eccentricity. The depth of the LISA survey reaches a redshift ~$5$ ($0.1$) for binaries with a primary black hole mass $m_1$ ~$10^4 M_\odot$ ($10^3 M_\odot$). If the orbital companion is a white dwarf, which could be disrupted prior to plunge, LISA's survey depth is well matched to (and, in many cases, exceeds) the one of electro-magnetic surveys. Although the maximum distance at which a source can be detected depends weakly on the orbital eccentricity, the latter strongly affects the portion of the binary inspiral over which a source is detectable. The instrument's sensitivity time-volume varies by many orders of magnitude depending on the binary's component masses: it reaches ~$1 - 10^3 Gpc^3 yr$ (~$10^{-2} - 10^3 Gpc^3 yr$) for the more massive systems with $m_1 = 10^5 M_\odot$ ($10^4 M_\odot$) and decreases to ~$10^{-4} - 1 Gpc^3 yr$ for lighter primary black holes with $m_1 = 10^3 M_\odot$. Importantly, from tens of percent to the overwhelming majority of the total sensitivity time-volume (and therefore number of potential detections) comes from sources that do not plunge during the yr-long mission lifetime and are observed at an earlier stage of their inspiral. Despite the poorly known merger rates of this class of sources, our results show that LISA could identify from a handful to ~$10^3$ intermediate-mass black holes providing a new observational avenue for studying these elusive objects and the environments in which they reside.

2611.12594.abstract: Stars form in clustered environments, and then the stars may congregate into star clusters. The timescale on which individual stars form is not necessarily the same as the timescale on which star clusters assemble. Therefore, developing methods to probe these different timescales is a crucial part of understanding star cluster assembly and early evolution. Dynamical ages can be constructed from the kinematics of individual stars in clusters in the solar neighborhood using Gaia data. Using a star formation simulation, we test five different dynamical age methods. We divide dynamical ages into two approaches: methods which trace the size evolution of the cluster, and methods which trace the trajectories of individual stars. We confirm that size methods cannot accurately derive ages in bound clusters whereas methods tracing individual stars can be applied to both bound and unbound systems. We find that different dynamical age methods trace different epochs of star cluster formation and assembly: The method using stars with the oldest traceback ages provides an upper limit on stellar ages and the method using the median traceback ages is the best proxy for isochronal ages. Methods which trace the size evolution of the cluster best trace the onset of cluster expansion. Our work suggests that the median traceback time of stars moving away from the cluster provides the most reliable proxy for isochronal age, and that this method can be applied to any expanding system.

2611.12595.abstract: A model of warm, dissipative corona on top of an accretion disk is investigated, to explain the soft X-ray excess (SXE) emission observed in active galactic nuclei (AGN). The final ray-traced spectrum, computed through photoionization code with Comptonization, accounts for both: emitted and reflected components. As a result, the strength of the SXE depends on the radial extend of the warm corona, i.e., its outer edge. We show that the radial transition from warm corona to disk atmosphere is governed by line cooling. By moving away from a central black hole Compton cooling is gradually replaced by line cooling, and the temperature drops sharply in vertical direction at a narrow iron ionization front, where iron ions Fe \textsc{xxv}--Fe \textsc{xxvi} recombine to Fe \textsc{xvii}. Notably, this transition takes place at a particular value of internal heating $\approx 1.6 \times 10^{-23}$ erg cm$^{3}$ s$^{-1}$, regardless of the Eddington ratio. We show, that at the given metal abundance, the SXE emitting area is larger for a higher accretion rate, in agreement with recent findings in changing look AGN. The overall emission spectrum from a warm corona is featureless, and the only iron K$_{\alpha}$ line comes from a reflection. The line is stronger and more gravitationally distorted for a lower accretion rate, which is a direct result of the size of the warm corona. Furthermore, by increasing the iron abundance, the iron ionization front moves closer towards black hole, and a stronger iron line complex is emitted locally.

2611.12831.abstract: Gravitational collapse and instability, black-hole dynamics in systems with large scale separations, and questions surrounding extremal black hole formation require full nonlinear studies using accurate and adapted numerical tools. To this end, we present a new algorithm to study collisionless relativistic systems using a fully kinetic description of matter coupled to the evolving spacetime. In detail, we present a numerical-relativity particle-in-cell (NRPIC) framework for solving the Einstein--Vlasov system in three spatial dimensions. Implemented on top of the performance-portable \texttt{AthenaK} code, the method couples particle dynamics to Z4c spacetime evolution in moving puncture gauge through conservative stress-energy deposition on adaptively refined meshes. Our implementation makes use of advances in the computational modeling of relativistic plasmas using modern PIC models, now made available to general-relativistic gravity via an equivalent electrodynamic formulation. We introduce a Boris-type particle pusher that exploits the electrodynamic (Lorentz force) form of the geodesic force. We validate the coupled evolution against spherical dust collapse, follow prolate collapse through collisionless caustics into black-hole formation, and investigate the stability and nonlinear migration of relativistic clusters. Highlighting its potential to study gravitational instability in NR, we simulate the collapse of two overdensities within a common collisionless envelope, following black-hole formation, binary inspiral and merger, and subsequent mass accretion onto the remnant.

2611.12841.abstract: We present uniform posteriors indicating the presence or absence of stellar and planetary companions over a sample of $10^5$ stars in Hipparcos and Gaia. We use the "G23H" catalog to fit a model that incorporates absolute astrometry constraints from Hipparcos, Gaia DR2, and Gaia DR3, as well as Gaia DR3 photometry, excess RV variability, and includes information from the presence or absence of common-proper motion companions. The resulting posteriors can be used directly to detect new companions, to target RV and imaging follow-up observations, and for downstream demographics studies. We highlight example detections of known and new candidate companions and the companion detection rate across the HR diagram. The modelling approach we present is directly applicable to Gaia DR4 epoch astrometry and RVs. All posteriors are provided as a machine-readable catalog and user-accessible website this http URL.

2611.12845.title: AGN Feedback Turbulence in Cool-core Clusters: Evidence from XRISM

figures.caption: Figure 1: Radial profile of the velocity dispersion (red points) in Perseus along the NW direction, measured from the XRISM Performance Verification (PV) observations. The measurements indicate the presence of two dominant kinematic drivers (XRISM Collaboration, 2026a): one powered by AGN feedback and the other associated with mergers. The corresponding theoretical models are shown by the light-orange and grey lines, respectively. The AGN feedback component is modeled as a uniform Gaussian random velocity field with $\sigma_{\rm agn}=150{\rm\,km\,s^{-1}}$, $\ell_{\rm inj}=20{\rm\,kpc}$ and $r_{\rm agn}=55{\rm\,kpc}$ (see Section 2 for more details). The shaded region indicates the standard deviation of the velocity dispersion in each radial bin from the turbulent simulation. The thick black line shows the total model, obtained by adding the two components in quadrature, which provides a good description of the XRISM measurements.

Figure 2: Predicted radial profiles of the velocity dispersion in Perseus for different extents of the AGN feedback region, $r_{\rm agn}=55{\rm\,kpc}$ (black, same as in Fig. 1) and $r_{\rm agn}=90{\rm\,kpc}$ (blue). The dashed and solid lines show the feedback component and the total model, respectively. The red points reproduce the Perseus data points shown in Fig. 1. The double-driver scenario can produce a relatively flat velocity dispersion radial profile (see Section 2).

Figure 3: Bulk velocity (top) and velocity dispersion (bottom) measured across the four quadrant subregions of the central XRISM/Resolve pointing of A1795 (red points). The bulk velocities are measured relative to the BCG ($z_{\rm BCG}=0.06300$). For comparison, the blue points show measurements from the two outermost annuli in the off-axis pointing reported by Sarkar et al. (2026). No significant bulk motions are detected in the observed regions, suggesting that AGN feedback on small scales makes a substantial contribution to the velocity field in the cluster core (see Section 3.1).

Figure 4: Same as Fig. 1 but for A1795. The red points show the XRISM measurements (Sarkar et al., 2026). The AGN feedback component (light-orange) is modeled with $\sigma_{\rm agn}=120{\rm\,km\,s^{-1}}$, $\ell_{\rm inj}=20{\rm\,kpc}$, and $r_{\rm agn}=105{\rm\,kpc}$. The merger component (grey; baseline model) is modeled using the same turbulent simulation as for Perseus. The profile extracted from an earlier snapshot of the simulation (blue) is shown to illustrate the potential systematic uncertainty in the merger contribution (see also Fig. 13). In either case, AGN feedback dominates the velocity dispersion in the core of A1795 (see Section 3.1).

Figure 5: Left panel: Simulated X-ray surface brightness distribution at $t\simeq 1.6{\rm\,Gyr}$, which resembles the relative positions of A2029 (the main cluster) and a southern infalling group (Sohn et al., 2019; Mirakhor et al., 2022, see). The white dashed line indicates the group’s infalling trajectory. The group is approaching its primary apocenter. Right panels: Zoomed-in maps of the X-ray surface brightness, X-ray-weighted temperature, X-ray-weighted LOS bulk velocity, and velocity dispersion in the region indicated by the black box in the left panel. The white circle approximately indicates the region covered by the XRISM central PV pointing. Our simulation broadly captures key X-ray features in A2029 (see Section 3.2).

Figure 6: X-ray-weighted velocity dispersions (solid points) measured within a radius of $\simeq 135{\rm\,kpc}$, approximately the XRISM/Resolve’s FOV at A2029’s redshift, along $500$ different sightlines in the $t=1.6$ and $2.6{\rm\,Gyr}$ snapshots, respectively. The sightlines are uniformly sampled over $4\pi$ steradians, with the inclination angle defined as the angle between the sightline and the normal to the merger plane. The horizontal yellow band indicates the XRISM measurement and its $1\sigma$ uncertainty. Open points show the velocity dispersion at $t=1.6{\rm\,Gyr}$ after excluding the bulk velocity contribution (see Section 3.2 for details). The sloshing-driven bulk rotation of the gas is the major source of uncertainty in our model of $\sigma_{\rm los}$.

Figure 7: Same as Fig. 1 but for A2029. The AGN feedback component is modeled with $\sigma_{\rm agn}=100{\rm\,km\,s^{-1}}$, $\ell_{\rm inj}=20{\rm\,kpc}$, and $r_{\rm agn}=120{\rm\,kpc}$. The large-scale component (grey solid line and shaded region) is derived from the tailored merger simulation for A2029 at $t=1.6{\rm\,Gyr}$. The overlaid dashed line shows the predicted merger component with the bulk-motion contribution excluded, providing a better comparison with the measurements beyond $\simeq 150{\rm\,kpc}$ along the NE arm (XRISM Collaboration, 2025d). Accounting for systematic uncertainties in the modeling, we can only place an upper limit on $\sigma_{\rm agn}$, which nevertheless indicates that the AGN contribution is subdominant to that of the merger (see Section 3.2).

Figure 8: Evolution of the radial profile of the LOS velocity dispersion for the A2029 merger simulation, viewed along the direction adopted in the best-match model. The grey band shows the same data as in Fig. 7, but binned logarithmically in radius. The elevated $\sigma_{\rm los}$ within $\simeq 40{\rm\,kpc}$ at $t=1.6{\rm\,Gyr}$ reflects the early stage of sloshing spiral development (see Section 3.2).

Figure 9: Gas entropy slices across the merger plane, illustrating the early evolution of atmospheric sloshing in our A2029 simulation. The low-entropy gas core ($\lesssim 50{\rm\,keV}{\rm\,cm}^{2}$) is significantly displaced from the gravitational potential center (white cross) for $\sim 0.8{\rm\,Gyr}$, increasing the central cooling time $t_{\rm cool}$ and the ratio of $t_{\rm cool}/t_{\rm ff}$. Our best-matching snapshot for A2029 is at $t\simeq 1.6{\rm\,Gyr}$ (as shown in Fig. 5), approximately $0.2{\rm\,Gyr}$ after the low-entropy gas returns to the central region. This is broadly consistent with the lack of cold gas but the presence of newly launched radio jets in the system (see Section 4.1).

Figure 10: A schematic illustrating the relative contributions of merger-driven and AGN feedback-driven turbulence to the velocity dispersion measured by XRISM in cluster central regions. Mergers inject substantial kinetic energy during core passage, which gradually dissipates (blue curve). The characteristic timescale over which a cluster is affected by a significant merger is a few Gyr, depending on its merger history. The red curve indicates the AGN feedback contribution, which may be quenched or significantly suppressed by the violent redistribution of the gas during the merger, but is eventually restored as the atmosphere resettles and cools. $\Delta t_{\rm q}$ and $\Delta t_{\rm r}$ denote the quenching and turbulence-refilling timescales, respectively. The sketch is not drawn to scale. A quasi-steady state of AGN feedback is likely established in relaxed clusters. The zig-zags are intended to illustrate the spatial and temporal variations in AGN feedback. We mark six galaxy clusters with deep XRISM observations in the sketch, including the two clusters analyzed in detail in this paper as well as Perseus (XRISM Collaboration, 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a), A3571 (Aihara et al., 2026; McCall et al., 2026), Centaurus (XRISM Collaboration, 2025a), and Coma (XRISM Collaboration, 2025b; Gatuzz et al., 2026).

2611.12845.abstract: The XRISM X-ray Observatory has revealed evidence for a "double-cascade" scenario in the Perseus cluster, in which active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback and mergers drive turbulence over distinct radial ranges and spatial scales. Whether this gas kinematic feature is common among cool-core clusters remains unclear. Here, we revisit XRISM observations of A1795 and A2029 to investigate the signatures of AGN feedback and their contribution to the gas velocity fields. In A1795, AGN feedback dominates the velocity dispersion in the core, similar to Perseus, and may provide turbulent heating at a rate comparable to radiative cooling. In contrast, we obtain only an upper limit on the AGN feedback contribution in A2029, where merger-driven motions dominate. Tailored simulations indicate that an off-axis minor merger $\simeq1.6$ Gyr ago displaced the central low-entropy gas in A2029, potentially suppressing AGN activity. This gas is now returning to the center, possibly facilitating the re-establishment of AGN feedback. We propose an evolutionary view of the double-cascade scenario, in which merger-driven motions dominate during and shortly after significant mergers, while feedback-driven turbulence re-emerges in cluster cores as systems relax. This framework provides a basis for interpreting XRISM kinematic measurements of (weak) cool-core clusters. Our findings highlight the importance of spatially resolved gas kinematics and detailed modeling for identifying double-cascade features and disentangling the contributions of AGN feedback and mergers.
